articles.content:
Cravath, Swaine & More: Cravath unveiled its new salary scale running from $235,000 to $440,000 and special bonuses of up to $40,000, topping Milbank’s numbers (though Milbank’s been paying for months at this point).
Scoreboard: Check out all the raises and bonuses here.
What’s In A (Domain) Name?: Dueling domain registrations pair Cahill Gordon with both DLA Piper and Willkie, fueling speculation over who might rescue the 107-year-old firm.
Rules Of Professional Responsibility? Never Heard Of Her: Southern District of Texas U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz earned a bar grievance over his letters harassing Democratic lawmakers and responded by promising more frivolous threats.
Weil Of Fortune: Simpson Thacher leads the scramble for former Weil partners with 31, followed by Skadden, Sidley, Gibson Dunn, and Milbank, with 18 firms getting a piece so far.
Truth Social Contract: Kirkland clocked around $11.8 million in free legal services for the Trump administration.
Conjunction Junction, What’s Your Dysfunction?: The New York Times says Heller rests on a misquote, but that’s wrong… it’s way worse.
Cruel Summer: Keker, Van Nest & Peters will stop extending full-time offers at the end of its summer program.
Skip To The Good Part: Some Biglaw firms have skipped screening interviews and sent 1Ls straight to callbacks in the midst of first-semester exams.

articles.title: The Billable Hour Wasn’t Invented To Make Biglaw Firms Rich
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

The billable hour is Biglaw’s profit engine and the associate’s eternal lament, so most people assume it was cooked up in some money-hungry corporate firm. But the lawyer credited with inventing it built his first timekeeping system a full decade before he ever joined a private firm, to solve a very different problem in a very different corner of the profession. Where was the billable hour actually born?

Hint: The inventor applied factory-style “scientific management” to the problem in the 1910s — and later wrote a landmark book on access to justice.

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Billable Hour Wasn’t Invented To Make Biglaw Firms Rich appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice
articles.content:
The other day, I gave a presentation to a group of lawyers and legal professionals about AI use and its benefits and risks. As is my practice, I stressed the need for law firms of any and all sizes to have strong AI-use guidelines. I stressed that these guidelines should cover things like which tools are approved for use, the need to protect confidentiality, and the need to verify all citations and other information from any AI output.
And of course, I also talked about the risks of not having an AI use policy. The risk of unauthorized or shadow use of unapproved tools, the risk of confidentiality breaches, and the risk of citations to hallucinated cases and propositions. My standard shtick.
But for some reason, it occurred to me right before this presentation that I should also mention an added reason for robust AI use guidelines. And that is that good guidelines could protect a law firm if someone goes rogue and fails to verify citations before filing them in a court document. I usually don’t talk much about this since it seems rather obvious. But as it turns out, I was prescient to do so.
On November 13, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued an order sanctioning a lawyer who signed a brief with hallucinated citations. But it exonerated his law firm because it had proper AI use guidelines in place.
The Wrong Way
Here’s what happened. A lawyer submitted fabricated quotations and mischaracterized legal authorities in a brief. After he was outed by the other side, he owned up to it. Sort of. He filed a “corrected” brief. That brief removed quotation marks from the original hallucinated citations. But it retained the inaccurate legal propositions. Good thinking, dude.
But there’s more. The lawyer blamed a paralegal (why do lawyers always blame the para?). Undeterred, he then tried to blame the other side for failing to engage in a meet and confer before it alerted the court. The court wasn’t impressed: “There is nothing to negotiate or compromise when an attorney submits false citations to a tribunal.” Duh.
And all the while he continued to insist (and probably with his outside voice) that the authorities were “real” and “support the arguments advanced.” As if saying it over and over somehow made it so.
Want to incur a judge’s wrath and get sanctioned? Here’s a good roadmap. As might be expected, the court gave short shrift to the arguments. It sanctioned the lawyer under Delaware’s version of Rule 11, but that was not the end of the story. What about the law firm?
The Law Firm’s Role
Delaware’s Rule 11, like its federal counterpart, provides that “absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or employee.”
The court also cited the Delaware Lawyers’ Rules of Professional Conduct, which require law firm leadership to make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance with ethical rules. It also referenced ABA Formal Opinion 512, which calls on firms to establish clear policies on permissible AI use.
That meant the judge needed to look at what the law firm did to prevent these kinds of things from happening. And when she did, guess what? She found the “exceptional circumstances” that relieved it of any joint responsibility for its rogue lawyer. She determined that the firm had undertaken “substantial institutional efforts to prevent the very problem at issue.”
The Right Way
The firm first barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools back in March 2023. In 2024, it formed a working group to evaluate GenAI tools and study the ethical guidance. In July 2025, it adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy. That policy required an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness.
But it wasn’t just the policy. The firm went further. It developed an internal training program addressing hallucinations and the recommendations of Opinion 512. And, said the court, it addressed the professional obligations “concerning competence, confidentiality, meritorious claims, candor, and supervision.” The program was so good that Delaware’s Commission on Continuing Legal Education accredited it for an hour of enhanced ethics credit.
As the court put it:
In short, [the firm] did the right thing. It warned of GenAI risks, established clear verification policies, and trained its personnel through a substantial, multi-layered approach. [The firm] acted reasonably to prevent GenAI misuse and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls.
That’s an important lesson. Having an AI policy isn’t enough. You have to make it real.
Two Legs Of A Three-Legged Stool
The judge’s order and the firm’s actions clearly show that AI use guidelines, to be effective, must be a three-legged stool.
First, the policy itself must be thorough and robust. It must address all the things that the Delaware law firm addressed in its policy. That includes what tools are approved for use, how to protect confidentiality, and, above all, the requirement that lawyers verify the outputs. But that’s only the first leg.
The second leg involves training and education. Without it, the policy’s protections for the firm are moot. Here’s why: lawyers are naturally skeptical and independent. Most of us believe we are special snowflakes as well. So imposing rules on us without explaining the why and without being transparent about them will lead to disaster. Not only will it breed disrespect for the rules and management that impose them, but lawyers will simply look for ways around them.
And there is another reason why education is important. Most lawyers are busy. They are constantly dealing with deadlines and client pressures. So if given the opportunity, they will choose the path of least resistance to get work done. The rules be damned. I recall once upon a time being told that I was to use the firm’s VPN at all times when working remote. The problem was, using that VPN was slow and clunky. It was a pain in the ass. So you can guess what path I would choose, especially when under the gun. It may not have been the best choice, but it’s what happens when policies collide with the realities of getting work done.
The point is if the firm’s approved GenAI tools are slow and clunky, you can rest assured that lawyers will jump to tools that aren’t. That’s why education and training are key. That’s in part why the Delaware judge exonerated the firm. It had provided the training and the why for its rules, even if one rogue lawyer chose not to follow them.
But There’s A Pesky Third Leg
But the AI use guideline stool has a third leg as well. A leg which the Delaware firm also recognized as it evolved its guidelines over the years. AI use guidelines simply aren’t a check-the-box task. To be effective, they have to be evergreen. They have to evolve with the times. If you created guidelines in 2023, for example, it’s unlikely that those guidelines would have addressed the use of AI agents. Yet today, that’s a use that’s getting more and more common.
This means that firms must do something that many don’t like to do. They need to have someone, or perhaps several someones, keep up with AI developments, risks, and the evolving law. That means someone must spend nonbillable time monitoring those developments and ensuring the guidelines are frequently revised.
That brings us to something else a lot of law firms don’t do very well. It’s not enough for someone to recognize the need for guidelines to be revised. The firm must have a mechanism to approve those revisions that doesn’t take six months and involve never-ending partner meetings.
It’s Not A Choice
It’s complicated, no? Drafting guidelines. Training. Keeping up with rapidly occurring developments. All nonbillable. It might be tempting, therefore, for a law firm to throw up in hands and conclude sanctions are going to happen. That they are just a cost of doing business. A cost will be less than the value of the time spent on guidelines.
But in a world where judges are growing increasingly impatient with hallucinations in court filings, that’s dangerous. Not to mention the fact that hallucinations could lead to embarrassment, potential malpractice claims or, at the very least, unhappy clients.
So it’s really not a choice. Law firms absolutely must have AI use guidelines. They absolutely must train partners, associates, paralegals, and legal professionals, and everyone else in the firm, for that matter, about those guidelines and why they’re necessary. They absolutely must keep those guidelines up to date to deal with new developments. They absolutely must have a mechanism for promptly approving needed revisions.
That’s simply a cost of doing business in these days and times, so roll up your sleeves and get to work.
And by the way, the monetary sanctions imposed by the Delaware judge? She made sure the lawyer paid them out of his own pocket.
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.
The post AI Use Guidelines: It’s Complicated. It’s Also Not A Choice appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Some Law Firm Names Are Simply Too Long
articles.content:
Lawyers understandably have a certain amount of pride when it comes to seeing their names on the doors of law firms. Indeed, many lawyers work their entire careers with the hope that they will one day become a named partner of a law firm and have their name adorn letterhead, business cards, and other materials associated with a law practice. Moreover, adding a lawyer’s name a law firm can be an effective way to recognize that attorney’s contributions to a practice without necessarily altering the financial arrangements among the partners. However, some law firm names are simply too long. Law firms should generally have no more than four names for a variety of practical reasons.
Earlier in my career, I worked at a law firm that had four names. Although the name of the firm was somewhat lengthy, it was not particularly difficult to recite the name of the firm when answering the phone or introducing myself to other lawyers. At some point during my tenure at this law firm, the firm added a fifth name.
For whatever reason, adding that fifth name made it exponentially more difficult to say the name of the law firm. One would think that adding another name would only make it marginally more cumbersome to recite the name of the firm. However, there seems to be a point at which a law firm’s name becomes too much of a mouthful, and in my experience, the distinction between four and five names can be surprisingly significant.
This can be especially annoying for lawyers who need to identify themselves and their law firms numerous times throughout the day. When appearing in court, lawyers often need to state their names, the name of their law firm, and the parties they represent. When leaving voicemails, lawyers typically recite the name of their law firm and their contact information. Of course, receptionists and other law firm personnel who answer the phones at law firms might need to say the name of a law firm dozens of times a day, and having a particularly long law firm name can make this task more burdensome than it needs to be.
There are also a number of administrative reasons why law firms should have shorter names. From time to time, I need to write checks payable to other law firms in connection with litigation and other matters. Some law firm names are so long that it is difficult to fit the entirety of the law firm’s name on the line of a check designated for the payee. Although fewer people write checks these days, the legal profession still involves a surprising amount of check writing, particularly when it comes to disbursing settlement proceeds and handling escrow funds.
Long law firm names can also create issues when completing forms, preparing signature blocks, and populating fields in computer systems that were apparently not designed with the naming conventions of the legal profession in mind. Moreover, the more names that are included in the name of a law firm, the greater the likelihood that someone will misspell one of the names or omit a name altogether.
Some law firms have wisely gone in the opposite direction and shortened their names considerably. Earlier in my career, I worked at dearly departed Sedgwick LLP, which at one point reduced its name from four names to simply Sedgwick. From the perspective of someone who worked at the firm, it was nice to be able to identify the law firm with just one word. Numerous other large law firms have similarly adopted shortened names for branding purposes, presumably recognizing that it is much easier for clients and others in the legal community to remember one or two names than a lengthy succession of surnames.
Of course, I understand that there are sometimes delicate political considerations associated with shortening the name of a law firm. Removing someone’s name from the name of a law firm might be perceived as a slight, even if the lawyer whose name is being removed has not practiced law in decades. In addition, when two law firms merge, both firms might want some of their respective names to be reflected in the name of the combined enterprise. Nevertheless, there should be some reasonable limit to how many names a law firm includes in its moniker.
Four names should generally be enough to recognize a number of the individuals who have made significant contributions to a law firm while ensuring that the firm’s name can be easily recited and written. If law firm partners are having difficulty deciding whose name should be the fifth name of a law firm, perhaps the best solution is not to add a fifth name at all.
Jordan Rothman is a partner of The Rothman Law Firm, a full-service New York and New Jersey law firm. He is also the founder of Student Debt Diaries, a website discussing how he paid off his student loans. You can reach Jordan through email at jordan@rothman.law.
